en: Preface:
Formerly, when the Great Master Changshui was expounding and interpreting the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, celestial jewel-flowers rained down on the day of his lecture.
The site where he composed his commentary was granted the name Lengyan Jiangsi Temple. People have praised the meaning of his sub-commentary as being concise in expression yet rich in significance.

The details are exhaustive and the principles are profound; it synthesizes the strengths of various masters from the Tang dynasty, such as Huizhen and Minjiao, and encompasses the essentials of Xianshou’s Five Teachings and the *Awakening of Faith*’s five stages. Among the renowned commentators, he is still esteemed to this day.

Master Guangdu succeeded to the lineage of Xianshou and bore the burden of the doctrinal tradition, presiding over the lecture hall for more than thirty years. I have invited him to serve as its principal.
In his sandalwood quarters, with a vase of flowers and water for his alms bowl, he lived in serene seclusion behind closed doors, dedicating himself to the task of commentary for several years now.

The refined elite of the capital have long held him in high esteem, regarding him as the equal of Changshui. Regarding the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Original Life and the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground)...
The phrasing is fluent and the underlying intent is profound; from the Tang dynasty to the present, no commentary has been produced.
Having examined and verified the various scriptures and synthesized the various treatises, I have engaged in meticulous study and quiet contemplation, verifying all through the seal of the One Mind.

Following the structural divisions and classifications established by Changshui for the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, I have composed this commentary in eleven fascicles. Out of deep self-effacement, I have titled it the "Shallow Commentary."
He requested that I write a preface for it. I observed his opening commentary on the four debts of gratitude;

his words concerning the relationship between ruler and subject and father and son were like the distant bell awakening at dawn or the solitary horn blowing through the frost—one could not help but feel the depth of their evocative power.

As for the chapters on the stainless nature and the *āraṇya* (forest retreat), they were like a cicada on an ancient tree or a clear chime in an empty mountain; one felt a sense of being dazed, as if having lost something essential.

After a long time, when one observes the mind (*cittāvalokana*), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) manifests before them; when the illness is cured, both emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and existence (*bhāva*) are simultaneously extinguished.
Then, like the solitary brightness of the autumn moon and the distant azure of the cold river, one stands transcendentally beyond the realm of dust and dregs.

This principle emerged when the Emperor bestowed a title upon the monastery during the "Willow Flower" era, yet it is seen again today. Nevertheless, it is still called a "shallow commentary"—surely there remains something further to be expected from future sages.
Whether one who probes the profound and clarifies the obscure [is such a person], is not something I know. The Sūtra says: "The power of the merit of this sūtra is inconceivable;
it can cause the lands where it resides to be abundant and joyful. Thus, the merit of commenting upon the sūtra is truly sufficient to assist the sagely governance of the state for boundless eons.
How could it be merely for the sake of liberating sentient beings, but rather for them to universally realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Ti. This is merely to extensively repay the Buddha’s kindness; therefore, without hesitation, I have composed this preface as follows.
Written on an auspicious day in the second month of the spring of the Dingchou year of the Kangxi era by Prince Zhuang of Huosuo.
Preface.
I have observed that the sutras of the Buddha contain meanings that are exceedingly subtle, yet the Way they elucidate is most vast.
Being vast, heaven and earth are both encompassed within it; being subtle, emptiness and form are all reduced to a single principle.
The reason for this lies precisely in the diligent cultivation of the mind-ground, so as to contemplate spiritual transformation until nothing remains unmanifested. Therefore:

The Great Digest (*Dàchão*) compiles various sutras and treatises on the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*), manifesting boundless great compassion and demonstrating manifold methods for secret awakening.
It states that "the mind is itself the Buddha, and the Buddha is itself the mind"—these words truly deserve to be called a clear mirror.

Yet, though one may recite the scriptural treasury verbally, one is immediately obstructed at the ford of delusion; though one receives the Dharma-precepts through the body, the true source remains unawakened. [This] is merely a distant conjecture.
Enlightenment is as obscured as the long night; were it not for the profound mechanisms of the sūtras, one would be unable to awaken to the Zen school.
Furthermore, if the abstruse meanings had not been fully explored, one would have remained mired in delusion and fallen into error.

Thus, how could the merit of those who comment on the sūtras for the Buddha’s followers be considered slight? Dharma Master Guangdu has extensively studied the various sūtras, probing the depths and grasping the essentials, embodying...

The exemplary teachings of the Worthy One (Bhadramukha) employ the spiritual brilliance of a single individual so that all myriad principles are gathered within the heart; they do not differ from a mere floating resonance.

Responding to conditions to expound the Dharma, he has held high the banner of the Law for thirty years without ever leaving his seat, striving not to fail his own resolve and personally embodying the Great Way.
Among these, the *Cittabhūmi-darśana-sūtra* alone possesses a profound and deep-reaching purport.

There was no existing commentary to rely upon. It was for this reason that the Dharma Master resolved his mind to endure hardship, examining various sutras and śāstras over three years until the annotated work was finally completed.
In the early autumn of the year Bingzi, as he was about to entrust it to the carvers, he requested a preface from me.
I have long known that the Buddhist teachings are subtle and profound, and the words of the sutras are secret and deep, like gazing at the heavens where their height cannot be measured.
It is like probing the ocean, where its limits cannot be fathomed; how, then, could one with the narrow vision of a tube through a keyhole presume to offer a single word of judgment?
Upon reading his commentary, the principles are linked like pearls and the meanings are joined like jade discs. Unable to restrain myself, I struck my breast in joy and exclaimed:
"Most perfect! Most complete! The subtlest details of the Sūtra have been fully brought forth. For those who investigate the mysteries and enter the Way, this is a comparison [to the original].

It is as clear as looking at the palm of one's hand. Were it not for cultivating the mind-ground to refine one’s contemplative visualization (*dhyāna*), and through such visualization to dissolve the barriers of the mind-ground, there would be no faculty that could penetrate through.
How else could one reach this state? From this, one further understands the greatness of the meaning of the Sūtra:
it can encompass heaven and earth; its subtlety can be so perfectly integrated that it is indistinguishable from the whole.

Regarding the characteristics of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), [the Master] then cited the *Mahā-śāstra* and various scriptures concerning the essential purports of Nature (*svabhāva*) and Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), as well as the three roots and nine grades of the *pāramitās*, and the one virtue and four practices of the Unsurpassed Way.
Thus, he made the mind and the Buddha clearly manifest as myriad differences unified by a single thread.
Is the Dharma Master not truly one among the Greatly Awakened? I respectfully submit these humble words, feeling no shame for my own ignorance and meanness.

This is also intended to propagate the Buddha’s teachings so that the Way may endure imperishably, as brilliant as the sun and stars, awaiting the self-awakening of all sentient beings. Thus it is said.
An auspicious day in the first month of autumn, in the year of Bingzi, the thirty-fifth year of the Kangxi era.
Original Inscription by the Lord of the Half-Niche, Prince Duoluo Hui (Tāra-hui):
Preface to the Light Commentary on the *Sūtra of the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground*.
Since my childhood, I have known of this sūtra; having entered the Gate of Emptiness, I have occasionally perused it, only then beginning to understand its text.

His speech was fluent and his underlying intent was profound and far-reaching; yet, whenever he sought to understand its subtle mysteries, he would immediately become utterly bewildered and find no foothold.
This was because he had not grasped where the true meaning lay. Consequently, he traveled everywhere to consult learned masters and attended lecture halls without a single day’s absence.
Whenever I perused various Mahāyāna sūtras and treatises on the nature of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and so forth, there was nothing I did not hear; yet this single sūtra alone could not be heard.
Why was this? It was truly because no commentary or explanation existed. For this reason, the school of teaching did not transmit it.

People did not understand the meaning [of his work]. Consequently, he felt moved by a sense of lamentation and resolved to provide an explanation. However, because the necessary tools had not yet been perfected, he could do nothing more than increase his own shame.

Thereupon, he extensively studied the various scriptures and attained spiritual insight into the various treatises. When he was about to take up his pen, he was still hindered by his duties at the lecture hall.
For thirty years, he had failed to fulfill this vow. This is what is meant by saying that the Dharma does not respond in vain.
There must surely come a time for this. In the spring of the Guiyou year, during a moment of leisure from my duties as a guest, I once again investigated the teachings of Shenhui.

Suddenly, everything became clear and penetrated me; I attained awakening to the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground. Having cut off the flow and reached the shore, through a single thought of cultivation, the mind itself is Buddha.
Thus, the Sutra says: "This Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground, once it passes through the faculty of hearing, one should collect the thoughts and contemplate the mind, perfuming [the seeds]..."
The seeds of Bodhi will, before long, attain unsurpassed Bodhi. It is further said that within the three realms, the mind is sovereign;
those who can observe the mind achieve ultimate liberation, while those who cannot observe it remain ultimately submerged in saṃsāra.
Thus, one knows that the Gate of Contemplating the Mind-ground is the pivotal juncture for cultivation and the essential mechanism for entering the Way. Therefore, the Buddha’s—
Success or failure depends solely on whether the mind is capable of contemplation or not.

This is because all sentient beings possess within their own minds the ground of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, virtue, and marks; it is merely that these are obscured by material desires and deluded thoughts.
Yet they do not realize this themselves; thus, they carry treasures while wandering lost in their own land, clutching pearls while begging for alms.

When the Sage observes them, he truly deems them objects of pity. Thereupon, the World-Honored One, wishing to awaken this mind and guide them toward enlightenment, first speaks of the four debts of gratitude that ought to be repaid.
Desiring to clarify the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), he employs conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) to rectify this mind. Next—
The extensive praise of renunciation has already clarified the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); therefore, one now resorts to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) to resolve one’s aspiration.
Through the stainless nature, the *āraṇya*, and the subduing of delusion, one maintains and upholds the true. One delights in the practice of seclusion.
The "Exhortation to Fear" (*Kāruṇyapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) serves to discipline this mind; the Venerable Maitreya extensively sought out gates of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*) to cultivate this mind.
Furthermore, regarding the three roots and nine grades of the *pāramitās*, one is again exhorted that a true teacher is difficult to encounter.

Through the single virtue and four practices of the unsurpassed path, all are unified as the adornment of merit. This is the contemplation of the mind (*cittabhāvanā*) and the auxiliary divine mantra. If...

Myriad illnesses are healed by *āgata* medicine; attaining Buddhahood relies upon the contemplation of the seal. It is like a wind-blown sail unfurling upon a following current: the mind of bodhi is itself bodhi.
With the diamond armor as the function of the mind, one benefits both self and others, accomplishing the work of a single lifetime.
How sublime! That which is utterly beyond the reach of thought—can it be anything other than the Dharma-gate of the Sudden Teaching? Alas!

Alas! We now dwell at the end of the Dharma-Ending Age (*mofa*), when heterodox teachings proliferate in many directions. It is by relying on the preservation of this [text] that we may weigh and discern the correct view.

Furthermore, as it remained hidden within the scriptural repositories, it had not yet been widely propagated. Therefore, disregarding my own meager abilities, I have ventured to compose these commentaries, merely illuminating a single narrow opening to shine forth the gift of the Dharma.
I venture to hope that those of like mind will join me in repaying the Buddha’s kindness. Thus it is said.
On the Buddha’s Day of Joy, in the first month of autumn in the year of Bingzi, the thirty-fifth year of the Great Qing Kangxi era.
