Written by the śramaṇa Lai Zhou of Zhantan Monastery outside the Divine Capital, this preface to the exposition of the meaning of the sutra opens with ten sections:

First, the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching; Second, the classification within the scriptural collections (piṭakas) and teachings; Third, the delimitation of the principles and meanings.
1. The capacities of the sentient beings addressed by the four teachings; 2. The essential nature of the teachings that express [the truth]; 3. The general and specific purports of the teachings;
4. The sequence of the titles of the chapters; 5. The time and year of the translation; 6. A general explanation of the title; 7.
An individual interpretation of the textual meaning.
As for the general application of these ten gates, they began with Xianshou and flourished at Qingliang;

however, according to the specific meanings of the various sutras, each has its own degree of detail or brevity, as can generally be seen from works such as the *Huayan xuantan* and the *Mituo shuchao*.
For the present work, I shall list the names in accordance with tradition, while opening the chapters in a concise manner.

Now, regarding the arising of the ten gates: when a sage establishes a teaching, there must necessarily be a cause and condition for it; therefore, this is followed by the "Causes and Conditions for the Arising of the Teaching.

Once the principles of the teaching have been set forth, one must determine to which treasury (piṭaka) and vehicle (yāna) they belong; therefore, this is followed by the "Inclusion within the Treasury and Teaching.

Having known their classification, one must understand what the meaning and principles are; therefore, this is followed by the "Delineation of Meaning and Principles. Once the meaning and principles are clarified, [the text continues... that... has not yet...

Since it was not yet known who is the object of this teaching, the "object of the teaching" (*jñeya*) is presented next. Having understood those to be benefited, one may still be confused regarding the means of expression;
therefore, the "body of the teaching as the means of expression" (*vācaka-śarīra*) is presented next. Once the means of expression is understood, one may still be unclear regarding the ultimate goal;

therefore, the "general and specific aspects of the fundamental purport" (*tātparya-sāmānya-viśeṣa*) are presented next. Although the direction of the teaching is recognized, the specific categories remain unexamined; therefore, the "categories and their sequence" (*padārtha-krama*) are presented next. Now that...

The "Chapter on Enumerating the Contents" follows, as the translations and their translators have not yet been clarified. Next comes the "Periods of Translation and the Ages of the Translators," because although the doctrines and meanings are known, the essential outlines have not yet been clarified.
Following that is the "General Explanation of the Title," for even though the meaning of the title is understood, it is difficult to discern when confronted with the actual text.

Thereafter comes the "Detailed Interpretation of the Textual Meaning. The first eight sections constitute the "Gates of Meaning," while the final two provide the exegesis of the scripture; this corresponds to the Fivefold Profundity of Tiantai.
Regarding the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), there are few variations in detail or brevity. Its meanings are like a string of beads used to explain the various sutras; they all share the same intent.

First, concerning the "Causes and Conditions for the Arising of the Teaching": this refers to the purpose for which the Sage established the teaching. Furthermore, it contains both general and specific aspects.

The general principle applies to the teachings of the One Great Vehicle throughout all time. Whether responding to causes or responding to requests, manifesting principles or delivering sentient beings—all sūtras are thus.

The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world for the sake of one great causal matter: to open, reveal, awaken, and lead others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
This constitutes the general condition for all sūtras. This present sūtra, by means of the gate of contemplating the mind-ground, [fulfills this purpose].

Entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is specifically addressed in this sutra; herein, ten aspects are briefly shown: first, to admonish the delusions of ordinary beings so that they may personally understand cause and effect;
second, to directly show that the dharma-realm is not separate from the mind-ground; third, to lead all ordinary beings and followers of the two vehicles to cultivate the Buddha-wisdom;

fourth, to manifest that the four debts of gratitude must be repaid, thereby inducing the arousal of bodhicitta; fifth, to turn back those who are perverse and rebellious so that they may develop faith.

1. Because it is the True Dharma (*saddharma*). 2. Because it demonstrates the bodhisattva practices and compares their relative difficulty and ease. 3. Because it encompasses the cultivation of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) for the dual benefit of oneself and others.

4. Because it subdues the deluded mind and perfumes the correct contemplation (*bhāvanā*). 5. Because it correctly elucidates the forest hermitage (*araṇya*) practice to sever doubt and generate faith. 6.
Because it presents both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings together to swiftly realize the fruit of Buddhahood.
First, as for the admonition for ordinary deluded beings who understand cause and effect: When the source is clear, the stream is pure; when the form is upright, the shadow is straight.

The retribution for good and evil is such that the fruit does not differ from its cause. That which is easily seen in the present, such as the relationship between form and shadow or source and stream, is believed without doubt even by the foolish.
That which is difficult to comprehend across lifetimes, such as the causality of good and evil, is still doubted even by the wise.

It is difficult to believe. Therefore, our World-Honored One, about to expound this sutra, employs the light of wisdom of identical essence to perfectly illumine the Dharma-realm, manifesting the beginning and end of a Buddha’s life and clarifying the destinies of good and evil, so that those present in the assembly may see these signs and have their minds awakened.
It is to have self-confidence without doubt.
Second, the direct indication that the dharma-realm is not separate from the mind-ground: the three realms are mind-only, yet sentient beings are deluded and do not recognize this.
All phenomena are but consciousness; this is what the Buddhas have realized and known for themselves.

Therefore, the Buddha emits a radiance that illuminates the entire Dharma-realm, demonstrating that the myriad differences between the sentient world and the physical environment do not exist apart from the square inch of the mind of both ordinary beings and Buddhas.
This is the true meaning of the World-Honored One’s auspicious patterns of myriad virtues emitting light to symbolize the Dharma.
Third, regarding the guidance of ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) in the cultivation of Buddha-wisdom: "Ordinary" refers to the sentient beings of the six realms;

"Lesser" refers to those of the provisional teachings of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). They are collectively deluded regarding the ground of the One Mind and remain perpetually entangled in the two kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

Therefore, our World-Honored One directly pointed to the wondrous mind and opened up true contemplation, desiring that those of the ordinary, external, provisional, and lesser vehicles may all equally realize *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.
The Sūtra says: "I now expound the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground to guide sentient beings and cause them to enter the Buddha-wisdom.

Fourth, regarding the manifestation of the four debts of gratitude that ought to be repaid and the elicitation of Bodhicitta: The Great Way is vast and profound; when those of inferior capacity hear it, they are bewildered by its words.
When it is adapted to specific needs, it is easy to perceive; ordinary people accept it and readily apply themselves to its practice. Therefore, our World-Honored One first...
The discourse on the four debts of gratitude to be repaid is intended as a teaching suited to the occasion; the exhortation to generate the aspiration for Bodhi is intended as the ultimate teaching.
This is precisely what is recorded in the sutra regarding the deliverance of five hundred elders, which constitutes the causal conditions from beginning to end.

Fifth, to turn back the perverse and rebellious so that they may believe in the True Dharma: that which turns one’s back on the Right Path is called "perverse," and that which opposes one’s parents is called "rebellious.
These are truly the instruments for creating karma and the conditions for falling into suffering.

Therefore, our World-Honored One demonstrated Right View to transform the perverse and opened the Way of Filial Piety to turn back the rebellious. This serves to eliminate the accumulation of evil—the causes of calamity—and to initiate goodness.
The scriptural passage concerning this causal ascent is precisely the account of the son of the elder Jñānaprabha.
Sixth, regarding the demonstration of the bodhisattva practice by comparing its difficulty and ease: one who gives rise to the mind of dual benefit is called a "bodhisattva";

this is the name for the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*) leading to the fruit of Buddhahood. However, while their minds are not different, their modes of cultivation may vary; therefore, our World-Honored One...
This clearly distinguishes between right and wrong, explaining the differences between the lives of householders and those who have left the home life.
Thus, it points out that practicing pure, quiet cultivation in an araṇya (forest hermitage) is easy, whereas entering the Path while living at home amidst worldly entanglements is difficult.
This is the intended meaning of the scriptural passages in the "Araṇyaka" and "Detachment from the World" chapters.

For those who cultivate the dual benefit of self and others for seventy kalpas, their career shall soar like the flight of a great bird across the ocean, such that the ninety thousand *yojanas* can be achieved;

if the Way relies upon the gates of practice, then the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* can be easily transcended. Self-benefit and the benefit of others constitute the path of the Bodhisattva—the Six Perfections and the Ten Perfections.
The vehicle of the Bodhisattva must necessarily involve leaving the household life to dwell in an araṇya; only then is it truly authentic.

To leave behind worldly toil and dust and to attain purity is the easy path for the initial resolve. The scriptural text refers to the *Pāramitā* chapter, specifically that which was requested by Maitreya.

Eighth, subduing the deluded mind. For one who cultivates correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), the deluded mind is the mechanism for birth and death, while correct contemplation is the gateway for entering the Path.
Those who turn their backs on correct contemplation and pursue the deluded mind are the ordinary beings of the six realms.

Those who subdue the deluded mind and enter correct contemplation are the sages and worthies of the three vehicles (*triyāna*). This is truly because contemplation possesses both provisional and ultimate aspects; thus, there are [different] vehicles.

While [conventional teachings] distinguish between the small and the great, this [teaching] now points directly to the ground of mind (cittaprakṛti), designating it as "Right Observation" (samyagdarśana). Where the deluded mind ceases is itself Bodhi;
when the wisdom of observation becomes clear, it is identical with the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). As the Sūtra says: "Within the three realms, the mind is the master.
One who can observe the mind attains ultimate liberation," and so forth.
The ninth section clearly elucidates how the forest hermitage (*araṇya*) dispels doubt and engenders faith.

Although the Buddha has explicitly shown that the forest hermitage is what those practicing the path to enlightenment (*bodhimārga*) should rely upon, he feared that their acceptance might not be sufficiently firm; therefore, he cites the testimony of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as proof.
From this cultivation and realization, one attains the fruit of the Way. This is why it exhausts the lingering doubts of the great assembly and increases the clarity of the mind’s aspiration.

As the Sūtra says: "Because it is that upon which all Buddhas of the ten directions rely, and because all Buddhas of the three periods of time attain the Way"—all of these refer to the mind (the *manas*).

Regarding the simultaneous presentation of the ten [teachings] of Exoteric and Esoteric Buddhism for the swift attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood: those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom may reach the Holy City with a single stride;
however, those whose wisdom is shallow and whose karma is heavy must surely practice both to eliminate delusions and hindrances. Thus, our World-Honored One...

Exoteric and esoteric teachings are presented together, and the primary and auxiliary practices are raised in equal measure. This is intended so that those of both sharp and dull faculties may all enter the contemplation of the mind-ground.
This is the underlying meaning wherever the sūtra-texts explain hand-seals (*mudrā*) and mantras. Thus concludes the section on the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching.

Regarding that which is subsumed within the two collections of teachings (*pitaka*), first the subsumption by collection is clarified, followed by the subsumption by teaching. Now, concerning the first, there are two types of collections:

first, the three collections; second, the two collections. A "collection" (*pitaka*) is so called because it contains and encompasses; that is to say, it encompasses all meanings that ought to be known.
The Three Piṭakas are: first, the Sūtra-piṭaka; second, the Vinaya-piṭaka; and third, the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
Now, regarding the first, the Sūtra, it is also called Sūtranta and also called Sūtra. These are all variations of the Sanskrit pronunciation, and their meaning does not differ.
Ancient masters translated this as "Kie-king" (Sūtra), meaning that it accords with the minds of the Buddhas above and responds to sentient beings below.

This is its nature. Therefore, it is called a scripture that accords with principle and harmonizes with capacity. The term "scripture" (jīng) has many meanings, yet when synthesized, they do not exceed the principles of penetration, inclusion, constancy, and dharma.
"Penetration" means to thread through and clarify the underlying principles. "Inclusion" means to sustain and guide according to the capacities of sentient beings.
"Constancy" refers to the unchanging path of all Buddhas. "Dharma" refers to the universal standard followed by the world. This brief exposition preserves two aspects and extracts four meanings.
The rest is extensive; it cannot be covered in full here.
Second, the Piṇaya-piṭaka is also called Vinaya; this is merely an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term. This is translated as "taming" (dāmyati).

"Taming" (dāma) refers to training the three karmas with the desire for purity, which constitutes the practice of observance (*kriyā-dhāra*). "Taming" (*vinaya*) refers to restraining all evils and not...

"Practice" refers to the observance of restraint (*śīla*). It is named according to the practice it elucidates; thus, it is called the "Treasury of Discipline" (*vinaya-piṭaka*). Alternatively, *vinaya* may be translated as "extinction.

This means that while one extinguishes unwholesome actions, it is through this that one attains the fruit of extinction by extinguishing the afflictions (*kleśa*). In Sanskrit, it is also called *śīla*.
Some call it *śītala*, which translates as "cooling," meaning that one leaves behind the feverish afflictions of birth and death and realizes the cooling of nirvāṇa.
It is also called *pratimokṣa*, which means "individual liberation. These are all alternative names for the Vinaya Piṭaka.
Regarding the three Abhidharma Piṭakas: *Abhi* is translated as "confronting" (*pratya*) and *dharma* is translated as "phenomena" (*dharma*). There are two kinds of phenomena:

first, the ultimate phenomenon (*paramārtha-dharma*), which is the principle of the eternal abiding of nirvāṇa; second, the phenomenal characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-dharma*), which refers to the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths.
Since the phenomena confronted are twofold, the wisdom that confronts them is also twofold. The first is... [confronting]... the ultimate.

"Facing" (abhi) means facing toward nirvāṇa. "Opposing" (prati) refers to contemplating the four noble truths before one; it is called *abhidharma* because it faces toward the fruit and faces toward its objects.
This is the general designation for the treatises, established based on that which they explain. It was translated in the old style as "Incomparable Dharma" (*anuttara-dharma*).
It is named after that which expresses supreme wisdom; it is also called *upadeśa*, which here means "discourse" (*lunyi*).

This is because the ultimate principles of the Buddha-dharma are elucidated through discourse, and it is from this that the awakening of wisdom arises. It is also named after the essence of that which expresses [wisdom].
These aforementioned Three Pitakas exhaustively encompass the teachings of the one great aeon and pervade all the various vehicles, both Great and Small.

Upon examining their respective subject matters, each has its own specific scope as well as general applicability. Speaking in terms of their specific scopes: the Sūtras expound the training in concentration (*samādhi*), the Vinaya expounds the training in ethical discipline (*śīla*), and the Śāstras expound the training in wisdom (*prajñā*).
Speaking in terms of their general applicability, they mutually intersect and include one another. Now, this present Sūtra properly belongs to the inclusion of the Sūtra Piṭaka.

It also belongs, by extension, to both of the two collections (piṭakas). If categorized according to the scriptural collection (sūtra-piṭaka), it contains all three collections, because the precepts are expounded within its three fascicles of verses, and because it contains formal discussions (vāda) in response to Maitreya’s questions.
Regarding the two baskets (*piṭaka*): first, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka; second, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. Based on the aforementioned three baskets, they are divided into two vehicles.
That which explains the Hīnayāna is called the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, and that which explains the Mahāyāna is called the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. As the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states:
These three baskets (piṭaka), being distinguished by the higher and lower vehicles, further constitute the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

If the baskets were divided according to the vehicles, there would logically be three; however, because Pratyekabuddhas do not rely on instruction and are included among the Śrāvakas when appearing in the world of a Buddha, they are thus divided into two.
This present sutra is subsumed within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, as it encompasses the latter. II.
All are fully contained therein. Furthermore, because there are those named Śrāvakas who practice [the path], it is subsumed under two teachings.
Now, the ocean of teaching is profound and deep; the clouds of Dharma are vast and pervasive; the light of wisdom is boundless; and wondrous eloquence is inexhaustible.
By means of words that are wordless, one elucidates the principle that transcends words; by means of speech that is unspeakable, one responds to the inexhaustible.

The pivot [of the teaching] is that which is received by those at the ultimate stage; it is difficult for ordinary minds to grasp. Now, relying on the power of principle and scripture, I shall briefly clarify the origins of its opening and closing.

As for those who propagated and expounded it in the Western Regions and the Eastern Xia (China), regarding the sacred words of a single lifetime, they either opened up the fundamental schools or divided the teachings.
Some directly interpret the scriptural text according to their respective insights, each having its own basis. There are five reasons why [the teachings] are not differentiated:
first, the principle is fundamentally of one flavor, for diverse paths lead to the same destination; second, a single sound universally responds, for a single rain universally nourishes all.
Third, it is the intention of the Sage of Sanuan (Sanghabhadra) that [the teaching] constitutes one great matter. Fourth, because there are differing interpretations for each individual passage.
Fifth, because the various methods of teaching have formed divergent branches and streams. For these five reasons, it should not be divided.
I fear that if it were divided, people would fabricate heterodox views and engage in competing disputes over right and wrong; therefore, non-division is considered the correct approach.
Regarding the classification of the teachings, there are also several meanings. First, although the principle is of a single flavor, the explanations vary in depth;

therefore, they must be classified so that one may understand the provisional and the real. Second, although the Buddha speaks with a single voice, the teachings differ according to the differences among sentient beings.

Third, the original intent has not yet been fully expressed, for there are differences in speech that follow the intentions of others. Fourth, the words possess both general and specific meanings, as they are presented according to explicit teachings.
Fifth, although provisional and ultimate [teachings] are distinguished, one must understand that the Buddha’s intention contains elements of opening and revealing.

For these many reasons, to open [the teaching] yields much gain and little loss, whereas to close it yields little gain and much loss. One need only empty oneself to seek the fundamental principle; do not...
It may be divided and categorized; how could this harm the essential purport? Therefore, I shall now divide it.

Regarding the masters of India and China, I shall briefly cite several schools to provide for observation and awakening. First, I will clarify the traditions of this land [China], organizing them into five gates.
Regarding the first position, that which establishes the teaching of a single sound (*ekasvara*), there are two masters.

The first is Bodhiruci of the Later Wei, who stated that the Tathāgata’s single sound simultaneously responds to ten thousand [beings], with both the Great and Small Vehicles being presented together.

The second is Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin, who stated that the Buddha’s single perfect sound (*pariṇispanna-svara*) is free from thought yet universally responds; it is the capacities of the listeners that differ. Of these two masters, in the former case, the Buddha’s voice itself possesses diversity.
Subsequently, they differ according to the capacities of sentient beings; each attains one aspect of the perfect sound (samyagghoṣa), yet both share the same intent of non-differentiation.
Second, regarding the establishment of two teachings: first, the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of Western Qin established the teachings of the "Half" and the "Full.

By the teaching of the Half-character, he meant the Śrāvaka Piṭaka, which explains the principle as not yet perfected, because its characters are incomplete. Second is the teaching of the Full-character.
This refers to the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, which is said to be complete in its exposition of principles because it is perfect in its terminology.

This judgment is based on the meaning of "half" and "full" from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, combined with the analogy of a young child learning to write. Furthermore, Master Yuan of the Sui dynasty [stated this].

The same principle applies here as well. Second, Master Yan of the Sui dynasty established the teachings of the Gradual and the Sudden. First is the Gradual Teaching, which accords with those of gradual enlightenment;
it arises from the small to the great, and its provisions include the teachings of the Three Vehicles. Second is the Sudden Teaching, which accords with those of sudden enlightenment.
One enters directly into the Great [Vehicle] without passing through the Small; this causes one to attain the Way instantaneously.

Although this is explained in terms of the capacities of sentient beings as having gradual and sudden approaches, the teachings spoken do not go beyond the Half and the Full [Tripitaka]. During the early Tang dynasty, Master Haiyin also established two types of teaching:
first, the "Crooked" (ququ) teaching, and second, the "Level" (pingdao) teaching. The "Crooked" refers to that which was spoken by Śākyamuni Tathāgata.

The *sūtras* adapt to the capacities and dispositions of beings, shattering attachments according to their conceptual reckonings. Through skillful means and intricate detail, they cause sentient beings to give rise to understanding.

For example, although the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* expounds the principle of the perfect, all-pervading, and ultimate, it sometimes reveals the real by means of the provisional, or reconciles differences to return to unity;

therefore, it is called the "crooked teaching" (*ku-chü-chiao*). As for the "level path" (*ping-tao*), this refers to the sūtras spoken by Vairocana, which accord with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and are level.

They are taught equally, as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Although there is teaching according to the capacities of beings to individually subdue them, all of it is skillful means that accords with the nature (*dharmatā*), expounded all at once and instantaneously;
therefore, it is called the "Teaching of the Level Path" (*pingdao jiao*). Fourth, the Qi dynasty recluse Liu Qiu also categorized two teachings: first, the "Gradual Teaching" (*jianjiao*).
Beginning from the Deer Park and ending at the Twin Trees, it proceeds from the small to the great; therefore, it is called the Gradual Teaching.

Second is the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*). This refers to the Buddha’s initial preaching of the *Avataṃsaka*, which is like the rising sun first illuminating the high mountains; therefore, it is called the Sudden Teaching.

Third, regarding the classification of the three types of teachings, there are also three schools. The first is the Southern School’s Three Teachings, referring to those established during the Qi dynasty.
Later, the various masters of Jiangnan established these three teachings to categorize the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata throughout his lifetime:
first, the Gradual Teaching; second, the Sudden Teaching. This was entirely the same as Liu Qiu’s system, with the addition of the Indeterminate Teaching.

Because the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* states that the Great Vehicle was taught within six years of the Buddha’s enlightenment—contradicting the notion that the Small Vehicle came first followed by the Great—the Indeterminate Teaching was established to resolve this difficulty.

This refers to certain individual sutras which, although not included within the sudden teaching, clarify that the Buddha-nature is eternally abiding; such are the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, and others.
These constitute the "partial and non-definitive teachings."

Regarding the gradual [teaching], there are differing opinions among various masters concerning its division into opening and closing phases. Some maintain that it consists of only two stages, namely the "half" and the "full. Others divide it into three;

this is the view of Dharma Master Yiji of Mount Wuqiu, who held that for twelve years prior [to the Nirvana Sutra], those seen attaining the Way were taught what is called the "Teaching with Characteristics" (xiangjiao).
Twelve years later, up until the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one sees emptiness and attains the Way; this is called the Teaching of Non-characteristics (*animitta-vāda*).

Finally, there is the simultaneous illumination of the Buddha-nature in all sentient beings, wherein even those with no capacity for faith (*icchantika*) become Buddhas; this is called the Teaching of Eternal Abiding (*nitya-vāda*).

This is largely identical to the "Three Periods of the Teaching" established by the Tripiṭaka Master from Tang. The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha was a native of Western India who, based on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, established the [Three] Turnings...
The teaching of the three wheels of illumination and retention is also largely identical to this, though with slight differences in timing.

Specifically, it is said that the teaching of the wheel of turning (*dharmacakra*) was expounded during the first seven years; the teaching possessing both the wheels of turning and illumination was expounded after the seventh year, because emptiness illuminates existence;
and after thirty years, the teaching possessing all three wheels of turning, illumination, and retention was expounded, because it simultaneously illuminates both emptiness and existence.

Because it maintains the previous two [categories], it may be divided into four. This refers to the Dharma Master Sengyue of the Song dynasty, who maintained that following the period of "formlessness" (wuxiang) and prior to the period of "eternal abiding" (changzhu), the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is designated as the "teaching of ultimate convergence.
This is because it brings together the three vehicles into one, whereby all myriad virtues are directed toward Bodhi.
Alternatively, it may be expanded into five, for which there are two schools of thought: first, the method of Daochang’s Huiguan; [and second, the method of Huiyuan].

The Master and others, regarding the period after the formless (wu-xiang) and before the ultimate convergence (tong-gui), designated the *Jingming* and *Siyi* [Sūtras] as representing the "suppression and exaltation" (*yi-yang*) of the teachings.
As for the second point, it refers to the aforementioned Lord Liu; he did not distinguish between suppression and exaltation, but rather took the *Dige* Sūtra as the beginning of the teachings.
He established the teachings for humans and devas.
Second was the Vinaya Master Guangtong of the Later Wei dynasty, who inherited and studied the Tripiṭaka of Buddhatrāta and likewise established three teachings: called Gradual, Sudden, and Perfect.
The first [the Gradual] is for those whose faculties are not yet mature; one first teaches impermanence and only later teaches permanence, first teaching emptiness and later teaching non-emptiness.
1. For those of such [gradual] capacity, it is called "gradual" because they proceed step by step in this manner. 2.

For those whose faculties are mature, all aspects—such as permanence and impermanence, emptiness and non-emptiness—are fully expounded within a single dharma-gate; since there is no further need for gradual progression, it is called "sudden. 3.
For those who have reached the highest attainment and are on the verge of entering the realm of the Buddha, one explains the Tathāgata’s unimpeded understanding (*pratisaṃvid*).
It is liberation, the ultimate fruit and virtue, the most perfect and secret dharma-gate of sovereign mastery; therefore, it is called "Complete" (Yuan).

This is also spoken of in terms of the sequential order of the transformative ritual; the underlying intent clarifies that those capable of receiving the sudden teaching at the present time must have previously undergone transformation [under the gradual teaching].

Therefore, it is said that "the faculties have matured," a phrase denoting superior attainment that encompasses both the stages prior to the bhūmis (pṛthagjana-bhūmi) and the levels within the Buddha-realm, which refers specifically to the bhūmis themselves.
During the late Sui and early Tang dynasties, the Dharma Master Jizang established the doctrine of three types of dharma-wheels based on the fifth chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
First, those who upon first seeing my body and hearing what I have taught immediately believe and accept it, thereby entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata;

this is the teaching of the fundamental wheel of Dharma (*mūla-dharmacakra*). Second, those who previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna, having now set that aside; this is the teaching of the secondary wheel of Dharma (*śākha-pratāna-dharmacakra*).

Third, I now also cause them to hear this sutra and enter the Buddha-wisdom; this is the teaching of the wheel of Dharma that gathers the branches back to the root (*śākhopasaṃhāra-mūla-dharmacakra*).

Regarding the fourth point, the establishment of the four teachings, there are briefly four schools of thought. First, Master Guangzhai of the Liang dynasty, based on the second chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, established the doctrine of the four vehicles.

He held that the three carts at the gate represent the provisional teaching of the three vehicles, while the equal distribution [of gifts] at the crossroads represents the true teaching of the Mahāyāna.
This is because even the ox-cart at the gate is identical to the sheep and deer carts, as neither can actually be obtained. All...
Because they lack substantial reality, and because all sons seek them, it is known that these three are all empty designations used as skillful means.
Thus, the former three constitute the Three Vehicles, while the latter one constitutes the One Vehicle.
During the two dynasties of Chen and Sui, the Tiantai Master Zhiyi, following the Great Master Nanyue Huisi, established the Fourfold Teaching (*caturvidha-śāsana*).

He stated: First is the *Tripiṭaka* Teaching. This teaching elucidates the principle of the four noble truths regarding the arising and ceasing of dependent origination; it primarily instructs the Śrāvaka vehicle while incidentally transforming Bodhisattvas.
Second is the Shared Teaching. "Shared" means commonality, for the three vehicles share in its reception. This teaching elucidates that dependent origination is [itself...]

Emptiness and the principle of the Four Noble Truths of non-arising constitute the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna; it is the primary transformation for Bodhisattvas while also extending to the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Those who wish to attain the Śrāvaka vehicle should study the Prajñāpāramitā," and so forth.

However, regarding the wisdom of teaching and realization, as well as the stages of practice, cause, and effect, these all encompass both the shallow and the deep, differing from the "shared Prajñā" which is shared only with [the two vehicles].
Shallow. Third is the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*). "Separate" means not shared; it is so called because it is taught for those who are not of the Two Vehicles.

This teaching correctly elucidates the principle of the immeasurable Four Noble Truths as provisional names based on causes and conditions. It specifically transforms Bodhisattvas and does not involve the Two Vehicles;

thus, when Śrāvakas are present in the assembly, they are like the deaf or the blind. While it is not called "not shared" [in the strictest sense], it is termed "separate" because it also intends to distinguish it from the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
Because the single cause transcends [others] and the single fruit is not integrated, one practices through distinct stages; thus, the integration of cause and fruit cannot be attained.

Fourth is the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). "Perfect" (*yuan*) takes the meaning of being non-partial. This teaching correctly elucidates the inconceivable dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the Middle Way between the two truths, and the fullness of both phenomena and principle.
Being neither partial nor distinct, it transforms only those of the highest sharp faculties; therefore, it is so named.
[The Perfect Teaching] is "round. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Manifesting the power of sovereign mastery, he preaches the Perfect Sūtra;

immeasurable sentient beings all receive the prediction of Bodhi," and so forth. Specifically, in the [three] provisional teachings, the doctrine, principle, and so on are all distinct; in the Perfect Teaching, the doctrine, principle, and so on are all round.

Furthermore, these four teachings arise from the three contemplations. Because there is a difference between analytical and intrinsic [emptiness] when entering emptiness from the conventional, there are the first two [teachings].
The arising of the teachings: there is the arising of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao), which proceeds from emptiness to the provisional and from the provisional to the middle;

there is the arising of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao), wherein the three contemplations are attained within a single moment of mind. Furthermore, these four teachings are not restricted to a single division, as multiple teachings may be contained within one division.
Moreover, they are further subsumed by the four modes of conversion (*huayi*): namely, the Sudden, the Gradual, the Indeterminate, and the Secret. The Sudden and Gradual are identical in this regard.
The former refers to Master Yu; the latter two refer to a single sound with different interpretations. If they understand one another, it is called "indeterminate";
if they do not understand one another, it is called "secret."

Third, during the early Tang dynasty, the Dharma Master Wonhyo of Haidong also established four teachings: first, the distinct teaching of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), such as the *Catuḥsatya-pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* and others;

second, the common teaching of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*; third, the partial teaching of the one vehicle (*ekayāna*), such as the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*;
and fourth, the complete teaching of the one vehicle, such as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. However, regarding the three vehicles...

The teaching shared [with others] is called the Triyāna (Three Vehicles) teaching. Within this, that which does not yet clarify the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is called the Teaching of Distinct Characteristics.

That which explains the emptiness of all phenomena is the Shared Teaching. That which is not shared with the two vehicles is called the One Vehicle teaching. Within this, that which has not yet manifested the Universal Dharma is called the Teaching According to Capacity.
That which fully clarifies the Universal Dharma is called the Perfect Teaching. However, this Great Master is largely identical to Tiantai; it is only that he merges them.
The distinction between the Separate and the Perfect [Vehicles] is merely the addition of the One Vehicle division.
Fourth, Master Yuan, a disciple of Xianshou, established four types of teaching based on the *Ratnagotravibhāga*. The treatise states:
"There are four kinds of sentient beings who do not recognize the Tathāgatagarbha, like those born blind: first, ordinary worldlings; second, śrāvakas; third..."

The Pratyekabuddhas. Fourth, the bodhisattvas at the initial stage of mind. Regarding the four teachings: first, the teaching of delusion regarding reality and divergent attachments, which corresponds to those ordinary worldlings;
second, the teaching of one part and a half of reality, which corresponds to those of the two vehicles;

third, the teaching of one part of the fulfillment of reality, which corresponds to those bodhisattvas at the initial stage of mind; fourth, the teaching of the complete fulfillment of reality, which corresponds to those who realize the Tathāgatagarbha. First...
The first refers to the various non-Buddhist schools (tīrthikas), who are deluded regarding the true principle and extensively give rise to heterodox attachments.

The second refers to the Hīnayāna, which, regarding the two aspects of the principle of *tathatā*—remaining unchanging while following conditions—speaks only of the principle revealed by the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*);

therefore, it is called "half," like the "half-syllables" (*ardha-kṣara*) in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The third refers to those who attain only the unchanging aspect but do not attain the aspect of following conditions; therefore, it is called "one part."

Furthermore, it is called "complete" because it explains both types of emptiness simultaneously. Fourth, it is complete in its two aspects of "changing according to conditions" and "remaining unchanging," as explained extensively therein.

Fifth, regarding the classification of the five teachings, there are briefly two schools. First, the master Paramārtha of the Tripiṭaka classifies them into four categories of teaching, namely: the Teaching of the Four Noble Truths... [as stated].
1. The Four Āgamas and so forth; 2. The Teaching of Signlessness, referring to the various Prajñāpāramitā sūtras; 3. The Teaching of Contemplative Practice, referring to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra; 4.
The Teaching of Peaceful Bliss, referring to the Nirvāṇa Sūtra, as it expounds upon permanence and bliss; 5. The Teaching of Protection, referring to the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra.
This is spoken in order to explain the matter of protecting the True Dharma.
Regarding the five teachings established by the two Great Masters, Xianshou and Fazang, they shall be understood below.

Second, as for the clarification of the Western Regions (Xiyu), this refers to the present-day schools of Nature (Xingzong) and Characteristics (Xiangzong), which originally emerged from that region; therefore, it is called the Western Regions.
This refers to Nālandā Monastery. At that time, there were two great virtuous masters: the first named Śīlabhadra and the second named Jñānaprabha.
Śīlabhadra inherited the lineage of Maitreya and Asaṅga from afar, and followed Dharmapāla and Sthiramati in his immediate vicinity.

Relying upon the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and other scriptures, as well as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other treatises, he established three types of teachings, taking the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* Mahāyāna as the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). This was precisely the tradition of the Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty.

The Master’s school asserts that when the Buddha first turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Truths of the Hīnayāna at the Deer Park, he taught that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) arise from conditions, thereby refuting the non-Buddhists' [notions of] causes such as self-nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, he taught that what arises from conditions is without self (*anātman*), overturning the non-Buddhist view of a self;
however, he had not yet explained the principle of the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). This refers to the *Catur-āgama* and other such texts. During the second period, although...
Based on the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty; this overturns the position of the Śrāvaka-vehicle.
However, regarding the *paratantra* (dependent) and *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) natures, they were not yet said to exist.

It was during the third period, in the various Prajñāpāramitā sūtras and others, that—based on the correct principles of the Mahāyāna—the three natures and the three absences of nature (*trividha-niḥsvabhāvatā*) were fully explained, which alone constitutes the exhaustion of the truth. These are, for instance, the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* and others.
Therefore, regarding those three periods: the first falls into the extreme of existence, and the second falls into the extreme of emptiness; neither is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

It is only at the final period that the parikalpita-svabhāva is explained as empty while the remaining two [natures] are established as existent; thus, by acceding to the Middle Way, it alone is of definitive meaning.
The second was the master Jñānaprabha. He inherited the lineage of Mañjuśrī and Nāgārjuna from afar and received the teachings of Candrakīrti and Bhāviveka from nearby.

Relying upon sūtras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* and treatises such as the *Madhyamaka*, he also established the doctrine of the three periods of teaching, regarding the signless Mahāyāna as the true definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
This means that at the beginning, in the Deer Park, the Buddha taught the Hīnayāna, clarifying that both the objective realm (*viṣaya*) and the mind (*citta*) exist.

Subsequently, during the middle period, for those of middling faculties, he taught the Mahāyāna of the Dharma-characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), wherein the objective realm is empty while the mind exists, according to the principle of *vijñapti-mātratā* (consciousness-only). This was because their faculties were still inferior and they had not yet been able to fully enter the equality of true emptiness.
Finally, in the third period, for those of superior faculties, he taught the Mahāyāna of Non-appearance (*alakṣaṇa*), analyzing the mind...
Subject and object are both empty; their equal, single flavor constitutes the true definitive meaning.

Master Xianshou established five teachings: first, the Hīnayāna teaching; second, the Initial Mahāyāna teaching; third, the Final teaching; fourth, the Sudden teaching; and fifth, the Perfect teaching.
The first corresponds to the *piṭaka* (Tripitaka) teaching of Tiantai. If categorized according to the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics) taught therein, it merely explains...

The seventy-five dharmas merely teach the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and do not teach the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Even where the emptiness of phenomena is briefly mentioned, it is not clearly elucidated.
Since they establish the roots of defilement and purity solely based on the six consciousnesses and the three poisons—as the *Āgamas* state:

"Greed, hatred, and delusion are the roots of the world"—they have not exhausted the source of all phenomena; consequently, there is much dispute and disagreement among the various schools regarding their tenets.
Second is the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna, also called the Partial Teaching (*bhinnadeśanā*).

This is because during the second and third periods of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, it was equally accepted that those of fixed nature among the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), as well as the icchantikas, would all fail to attain Buddhahood; therefore, these are now combined and treated as a single teaching.

Because it does not fully exhaust the principles of the Mahāyāna Dharma, it is established as the first [stage]. Since there are those who do not attain Buddhahood, it is called "partial. It extensively expounds the Dharma.

Regarding characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is explained in brief. The nature of phenomena thus explained is enumerated among the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*).

Although the numerical categories of phenomena thus explained are condensed from the extensive through analysis, there remain one hundred dharmas, which are clearly determined; therefore, there is little dispute. It is taught that there are eight consciousnesses, which are exclusively subject to arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*).

Based on these consciousnesses subject to arising and ceasing, the causes of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are established. As for the seeds of the natural order (*dharmatā-bīja*), their existence or non-existence is eternal.

It is distinct. Since the consciousness established [in the previous teaching] arises solely from karma and afflictions, the True Suchness (tathatā) established therein is eternal, constant, and unchanging;
it is not admitted to follow conditions.

Third, the Distinct Teaching (Triyāna-viniścaya-śāsana) is also called the Real Teaching (Siddhānta-śāsana). It holds that those of fixed nature among the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), as well as those of no-nature (icchantika), shall all eventually attain Buddhahood.
This marks the ultimate teaching of the Great Vehicle; therefore, it is established as the final stage. Because it accords with the true principle, it is called "Real" (Shi).

It explains the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*) sparingly and explains the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) extensively. Even the characteristics of phenomena that are taught ultimately converge back into this nature.

The eight consciousnesses established here are identical with the Tathāgatagarbha, which is established according to conditions. Thus, the arising and ceasing and the non-arising and non-ceasing are harmonized, forming a state that is neither [one nor the other].
They are neither identical nor different. All sentient beings are of one equal nature; they are simply True Suchness (tathatā) established according to conditions.

Being devoid of self-nature in their dependent aspect, they are precisely the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva). Since this single principle is uniform and level, it is said that the realm of sentient beings and the realm of Buddhas neither increase nor decrease.
There are many such categories of meaning, as explained extensively in the *Huayan xuantan* (Prolegomena to the Avataṃsaka).

Regarding the fourth, the Sudden Teaching (*tun jiao*): it holds that when not even a single thought arises, one is immediately named a Buddha. It does not teach by relying on the gradual progression through stages (*bhūmi*), and is therefore established as "Sudden.
As the *Siyi jing* (Saṃghāṭasūtra) says: "One who attains the true nature of all dharmas does not proceed from one stage to another stage. And the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says:
"The first stage is itself the eighth," and so forth, up to "What sequence can there be in the state of non-existence? Thus it is not [gradual].
This is accomplished through gradual stages as previously described; it differs from the subsequent stage of perfect integration and full virtue, and is thus designated as "Sudden.

Because it directly explicates this principle, it is called the Sudden Teaching (*dun jiao*). It does not generally describe the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), but solely elucidates true nature (*tathatā*).

Furthermore, there are no distinct characteristics of the eight consciousnesses; all that exists is merely deluded thought (*parikalpita*). The entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is solely beyond words.

The five dharmas and the three natures are all empty; the eight consciousnesses and the two forms of selflessness are both discarded. One reviles the teachings and exhorts detachment; one destroys appearances and extinguishes the mind.
To give rise to the mind is delusion; not to give rise to it is Buddhahood. Yet there is neither Buddha nor non-Buddha, neither arising nor non-arising.
This is the intended meaning, as exemplified by Vimalakīrti’s silence, which reveals the non-duality of phenomena.
Regarding the fifth, the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao): it clarifies that one stage is all stages, and all stages are one stage.

Therefore, the fulfillment of the mind of the ten levels of faith (shixin manxin) subsumes the five stages and achieves equal and perfect enlightenment. This is based upon the Dharma-realm of Samantabhadra, with its infinitely interpenetrating Indra’s net.
Because it is complete with both the principal and its attendants, it is called the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). This is precisely what is taught in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:

it is solely the inexhaustible Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), wherein the ocean of nature is perfectly interfused, and dependent origination is unimpeded. Phenomena mutually identify with and enter one another, like Indra’s net, layer upon layer without limit.
The subtle and minute contain one another, and the principal and its attendants are inexhaustible; for each of the tenfold dharma-gates individually encompasses the entire Dharma-realm.
It is already known that the five teachings encompass all sutras; however, it is not yet known under which teaching this particular sutra is subsumed.
If one classifies the sutra according to the teachings, it properly belongs to the Sudden Teaching (*dun jiao*), while partially belonging to the Final and Perfect Teachings (*zhong yuan*).

If one classifies the teachings according to the sutra, it fully encompasses all five teachings and further includes the Human and Celestial teachings (*ren tian*), because the principles and meanings of the five teachings as well as those of the Human and Celestial teachings are fully present within the sutra.

Third, regarding the delimitation of the meanings and principles: it is already known that this sutra properly belongs to the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*), while incidentally encompassing the Final and Perfect Teachings.
However, it remains unclear how the delimitations of these three teachings are distinguished. First, to clarify that it properly belongs to the Sudden Teaching:

within the sutra, the One Mind is suddenly revealed, leading directly into non-thought (*amanyana*) and the realization of right contemplation. This very One Mind free from thought constitutes the delimitation of the Sudden Teaching. *Awakening of Faith*.

The Treatise states: "That which is free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space. This refers to the True Dharma-realm (*tathatā-dharmadhātu*), one among the four dharma-realms.

Next, to clarify what is "incidentally inclusive," we first explain the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*). The Final Teaching is the ultimate Mahāyāna, which is the One Vehicle of the Shared Teaching (*sāmānya-yāna*).

Its scope is defined by the ten gates of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*dharmatā-vastu-avyāghāta-dharmadhātu*). In this present sutra, however, it exclusively reveals True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The single mind does not obstruct the cultivation and realization of the myriad practices; although these various practices are distinct, they do not interfere with the equality of the single mind.

This is the meaning of the ultimate, true limit. Next, to clarify the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao): this refers to the One Vehicle of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), which is fully endowed with the ten mysterious gates and possesses perfect, harmonious virtues.

This is found only in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Now, within this present sūtra, a small portion of that is briefly contained; therefore, it is said to "partially belong" [to the Perfect Teaching]. Thus says the sūtra.
It is said that Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, can contain a mustard seed; yet the King of Mountains and the mustard seed do not lose their respective characteristics.

This is precisely the "Gate of Sovereign Freedom regarding the Broad and the Narrow" among the Ten Mysterious Gates. There is nothing among humans, devas, or those of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) that is not fully encompassed therein.
However, because their respective limits are shallow, this is not explained in detail. Thus concludes the section on the delimitation of principles (*arthaviniścaya*).

Regarding the capacities of those to whom the four teachings are addressed: it is already known that the meaning and principle of this sutra are profound and vast; however, it is not yet understood for which types of persons they are intended.

To distinguish these appropriate capacities, I shall briefly divide this into two sections: first, the selection (liao-jian); second, the universal inclusion (pu-shou). As for the first, the selection, it is further divided into two parts.
The first clarifies those who are not suitable capacities (fei-ji), of which there are four. The first is "lack of faith," which refers to not believing in one's own mind.

1. Because they are unable to achieve meditative contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). 2. Ordinary fools are not suitable vessels; that is, because they pass their entire lives spontaneously, without recognizing the underlying principles.

3. Those with false views are not suitable vessels; that is, because they cling to the extremes of nihilism and eternalism, failing to comprehend the correct principle. 4. Those of fixed nature are not suitable vessels.

This refers to those who have severed their fetters through the voidness of ash-like extinction and thus fail to resolve upon the Great Mind. Second, the clarification of the primary capacity (*mārga*) also has four parts:

First, right faith is the capacity, for one who is willing to believe that their own mind can achieve correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*). Second, the wise person is the capacity, for they understand causes and recognize effects, and thus delight in cultivation and realization.
Third, right view is the capacity, for they clearly comprehend the ground of the mind and do not fall into the extremes of nihilism or eternalism. Fourth, the arousal of...

The mind is the capacity [for response]. To give rise to the bodhicitta is to transcend the partial and the limited. Second, regarding "universally encompassing": all sentient beings possess buddha-nature;

those who possess buddha-nature shall all attain Buddhahood. Although there are differences in the timing of when they give rise to the aspiration and the sequence in which they practice and realize it, as long as they possess the ground of the mind, they are all among the capacities for whom this sutra is intended. The above is according to the teaching.
The section on the intended audience is concluded.

Fifth, regarding the essence of the teaching that expresses [the meaning]: it has already been understood that this sutra’s intended audience is vast and extensive; however, it remains uncertain what constitutes the essence of the teaching that expresses it.

Now, I shall briefly clarify this by opening four gates: first, the gate of following appearances (*lakṣaṇa*); second, the gate of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*); third, the gate of returning... [text truncated]

The Section on Nature. The Section on the Four Unhindered Knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*). First, the characteristics are clarified: first, the elucidation of the expressive; second, the inclusion of the expressed.
This is because mere words without meaning do not constitute the Teaching. Regarding the first, the elucidation of the expressive: this refers to sound, name, phrase, and syllable. Sound is primary;
names are arranged in sequence to express the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena; phrases are established in sequence to express [the specific qualities of] phenomena.

Regarding the distinctions: the phonemes (*vyañjana*) are sequentially combined to serve as the basis for the preceding two [names and phrases]. These three—name, phrase, and phoneme—are the expressive manifestations upon sound;
for sound alone cannot express meaning, yet name, phrase, and phoneme have no intrinsic substance on their own.

Only when these four are taken together do they constitute the essence of the teaching (*śāsana*). As for the second point, the meaning expressed: if these sounds, names, phrases, and phonemes were without that which is expressed...

Regarding the meaning of these explanations, they are like the characters in the *Hai-pian* lexicon; they are not the sacred teaching itself. If there were meaning alone without text, there would be no basis for the principle.
It must be that meaning follows the text and the text relies upon the meaning; when text and meaning support one another, they constitute the essence of the teaching.
Now, from "Thus have I heard" until the end of this sutra, there is the substance of sounds, names, phrases, and syllables.

The *Xiuzheng Xindi Guanmen* (The Contemplation of the Mind-Ground for Cultivation and Realization) and so forth constitute the substance of the meanings they express. These two are mutually dependent; thus, the substance of the teaching is complete.

Since both the words and their meanings belong to the realm of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is called the "Gate of Following Characteristics. Second is the "Gate of Consciousness-Only" (*Vijñaptimātra*): because both words and meanings are transformations of consciousness, [they exist].
The four propositions regarding the original and the reflection: First, there is the case where there is only the original and no reflection; this refers to the teachings of the Hīnayāna.

This is because they do not understand that the teaching manifests from consciousness, asserting instead that the Buddha truly and substantially preached the Dharma. Second, there is the case where there is both the original and the reflection; this refers to the Initial Teaching (Śākyayāna).

This means that the words and meanings spoken by the Buddha manifest from the pure consciousness of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*); these are termed the "original essence" teaching. The words and meanings transformed upon the consciousness of the listener are termed the "reflection."

In the Image Teaching (Hīnayāna), because Buddhas and sentient beings serve as mutual dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for one another, the three [bodies] are merely shadows without an original. This is the Final Teaching (Mahāyāna).

Since there are no Buddhas apart from the self-minds of sentient beings, it is solely through great compassion and great wisdom acting as dominant conditions that Buddhas appear within the minds of those sentient beings whose faculties have matured to preach the Dharma. Therefore, the Buddha-teaching is entirely the mind of sentient beings.
The fourth is "neither original nor reflection," which is the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*). It is not merely that there is no Buddha outside of the mind;
even the images within the minds of sentient beings are empty. Because their nature is fundamentally beyond words, this is the teaching of non-teaching—without speaking and without hearing.

This is what is called true speaking and true hearing. Now, this sutra relies upon the two teachings of the Final and the Sudden, for the sake of sentient beings, those of the Two Vehicles, and bodhisattvas at the initial stage of the mind.

[Sākyamuni] and others perceived the Buddha within their own minds, and he preached for them the Dharma of Contemplating the Mind-Ground. This preaching is non-preaching, and this listening is non-listening;
it is the essence of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*). Regarding the gate of the nature of the Three Refuges: previously, the reflected images were subsumed into the eight consciousnesses;
now, the eight consciousnesses are subsumed into the one mind. Thus, nature (*dharmatā*) constitutes the body of the teaching. This "one mind" is the very substance of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Thus it is. From this True Suchness (*tathatā*), the teachings flow forth; therefore, one reunites appearances with their nature.

This refers to the suchness of the *geya* (verses), the suchness of the *vyākaraṇa* (prophecies), and the suchness of all twelve divisions of the scriptures. Tracing back through these stages in succession is like this:

for example, objects are not separate from dreams, and dreams are not separate from people. The *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* states: "The phenomena of birth are fundamentally non-existent; everything is but consciousness. Consciousness is like a dream."

Illusion. Since it is solely this one mind, the teaching-body (*śāstrakāya*) is taken as one's own mind. This sutra states that the Buddha taught that the three realms have the mind as their sovereign;
thus, observing this very mind is the teaching-body of self-nature (*svabhāva*). Regarding the four gates of non-obstruction (*catur-asaṅga-mukha*), there are two:

namely, the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai*) and the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shi-shi wu-ai*). As it is said, "that which is spoken is itself non-speaking," and "non-speaking is itself speaking"; both are the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena.
The meaning of "unimpeded" (*anāvaraṇa*) is as follows: it is like saying that one is many; the many do not impede the one.

This is the principle of the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena (*shishi wuai*), because mind and objects, principle and phenomena, all mutually penetrate one another. Therefore, it is called "unimpeded.

Now, this sutra takes the true-thusness mind-ground (*tathatā-citta-bhūmi*)—which is unimpeded by various practices and realizations—as its teaching-body (*śāsana-tattva*), precisely because mind and objects, principle and phenomena, are unimpeded.

Regarding the six points on the commonality and particularity of the fundamental tenets (*abhiprāya*): We have already understood the nature of this scripture as the expressive medium, yet we do not yet know its fundamental tenet; what is its meaning?

That which is esteemed in speech is called the "tenet" (*siddhānta*), and that to which the tenet leads is called the "goal" (*gati*). To clarify these tenets and goals, there are both general and specific aspects.

Generally speaking, the Buddhist teachings take dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as their tenet. Dependent origination serves to distinguish [Buddhism] from those who hold to the views of causelessness or false causes.

The teachings for a single lifetime are fully encompassed by causes and conditions; therefore, they are said to be "universal. If we restrict ourselves to this specific sutra, there are briefly four expositions.
First, at the beginning of the main body of the teaching, the Buddha speaks of the cultivation of the mind-ground, which serves as the primary tenet of his discourse, through which one attains Bodhi.

Taking refuge as the goal; second, the Buddhas cause one to repay their kindness, which serves as the primary principle for what is spoken; and the arousal of the bodhicitta, which serves as the goal of taking refuge.
Third, the elder Jñānaprabha’s repeated request to explain the four debts of gratitude serves as the primary principle for requesting the Dharma;

subsequently, the father and son seeking the Buddha to go forth into homelessness serves as the goal of requesting the Dharma. Fourth, the Tathāgata speaks of the araṇya, making reliance upon it the primary principle, and its cultivation...
Contemplating sudden enlightenment, one takes ultimate bodhi as the goal. This is a brief extraction of the major sections to clarify the destination and the path toward it.
Thus concludes the section on the general and specific scope of the primary tenets.

Regarding the sequence of the seven chapters: When the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, he necessarily relies on conditions for its arising. He emits light and manifests auspicious omens; doubts arise and there is a request to expound the Dharma.

Before the Buddha has emerged from his meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the Bodhisattvas provide auxiliary explanations to serve as the causal conditions for the teaching’s inception; therefore, this is called the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*).

Second, once the Buddha has emerged from concentration, he preaches the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground (*citta-bhūmi*). Five hundred elders, not wishing to hear the Great [Vehicle], are [taught] through the provisional exposition of the Four [Truths].

1. Because there is gratitude, there is the "Chapter on Repaying Kindness" (*Bao'en pin*). Next, because the Elder Jñānaprabha requested that the four kinds of kindness be explained again, there is the "Verses on the Gravity of the Four Kindnesses. 3.
Because the Buddha praised leaving the household life to cause one to be free from entanglements and bonds, there is the "Chapter on Renunciation and Abandonment" (*Yanshe pin*). 4.

Because the Buddha caused [beings] to dwell securely in the four dharmas and remain far removed from greedy seeking—this being the stainless nature (*vimala-dhātu*)—he spoke the "Chapter on the Stainless Nature" (*Wugouxing pin*). 5. Extensively...
1. He spoke of the *araṇya* (hermitage), exhorting and instructing [the disciples] in its cultivation and realization; hence there is the "Araṇya Chapter. 2.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One spoke of the merits of the *araṇya*, opening the way for its cultivation and realization; hence there is the "Leaving the World Chapter. 3.

Maitreya requested an observation, and the Buddha directed him to cultivate the Way by detesting the body; hence there is the "Detesting the Body Chapter. 4. The Buddha answered Maitreya’s difficult questions, elucidating the various *pāramitās*; hence...
There is the Chapter on the Pāramitās. Ninth, because one cultivates supreme merit by dwelling in an araṇya, there is the Chapter on the Adornment of Merit.
Tenth, because the Buddha’s discourse on the cultivation of the mind-ground has not yet been fully elucidated, there is the Chapter on Contemplating the Mind.

Eleventh, since the mind-ground has already been explained and the contemplation of dharmas has been clarified, there is further exhortation to arouse the bodhicitta and assist in the practice of divine mantras; thus, there is the Chapter on Arousing the Mind.

Chapter Twelve extensively elucidates mudrās and mantras to assist the power of contemplation and protect the practitioner, enabling them to swiftly attain Bodhi; hence there is the "Chapter on Attaining Buddhahood.

Chapter Thirteen details the beginning and end of the Mind-Ground, fully and clearly explaining cause and effect, principle and practice, entrusting it to those who are the proper recipients and ensuring its circulation for future generations;
hence there is the "Chapter on Entrustment. Thus concludes the sequence of the chapter titles.

Regarding the eighth section, the Dynasties of Translation: Since one already knows that the chapters and sections of this sūtra are as described above, one may wonder from what period its translation originated.

This Sanskrit manuscript of the sūtra arrived during the reign of Emperor Gaozong of the Tang dynasty, presented by a person from the Kingdom of Siṃhala, and was kept secret within the imperial palace.
It had not yet been translated when ten successive rulers passed by. It was only upon the accession of Emperor Xianzong that the Sanskrit manuscript was finally produced.

An imperial decree was issued for the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kaśmīra to preside over the translation, with eight scholars from the capital’s monastic academies serving as proofreaders and translators, including Meng Jian, a Palace Counselor.
Four men refined the text, compiling it into one work consisting of eight fascicles and thirteen chapters. Now, the Buddha was born in India, and his scriptures were all in the Sanskrit language;
without translation, who could have understood their meaning? Translation depends upon the person, and thus this work is produced to honor those of great meritorious service.
Although it is the person who can propagate the Way, it was not until this auspicious and favorable occasion that the wondrous response of the Buddha-dharma [could be fully realized].
It is established. One must believe that the Dharma does not respond in vain; a response must necessarily have its proper time. The designation of "dynasties of translation" emphasizes this timing.
Thus concludes the eightfold gate of meaning.
The Preface to the Brief Commentary on the Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Original Life and the Mind-Ground Contemplation is hereby concluded.
